title: Yŏja sanghaeng pʻyŏn
shelf_note: A vernacular Hangul manuscript (cursive, Korean letters including arae-a) of conduct instruction for women; it belongs on a Korean shelf.
structure_note: 62 pages, all with OCR, 33 translated. The OCR on three of the four sampled pages is a loop or an invention, so 'pages_with_ocr: 62' overstates the readable text. Page 48 shows the refusal string '[This page could not be translated due to content recitation restrictions.]' to readers as the translation. The catalogue language 'Korean' is correct here.

book_verdict: The OCR on this cursive Hangul manuscript fails: two pages are token loops, one is an invented homily repeated five times, and the fourth only partly matches the leaf. The English is fluent over that garbage and invents claims about the manuscript, such as calling a page a calligraphy exercise.
reader_summary: This is an 18th-century(?) Korean vernacular manuscript of conduct instruction for women, written in cursive Hangul. The transcription is not of this text: on most sampled pages it is a repeated word or an invented passage. The English cannot be trusted at all, because it translates the loops and adds notes about the manuscript that are false.

title: Hanʾgwa
shelf_note: A Korean manuscript of model pieces and topic titles for literary composition (parallel-prose memorials of thanks and congratulation), with red and blue reading marks. The text is literary Chinese written in Korea, which belongs on a Korean shelf.
structure_note: 150 pages, 135 translated. The catalogue says the language is 'Korean', but the text is Classical Chinese, so the language label is wrong (I7). One printed number repeats, but only 2 pages carry printed numbers, so this is probably a misread folio mark and not a defect. Page 133 lists topic titles only, so the book seems to mix model compositions with lists of exercise themes.

book_verdict: The script is legible and the OCR gets the shape of each piece, but it misreads names and allusions, and on one page it breaks into fragments. The English turns those misreads into invented people ('Zheng Shengchen and He Ergong', 'Mu Bopping') and into fluent prose over garble.
reader_summary: A Korean manuscript of model compositions and topic lists for formal memorials of thanks and congratulation, drawing on Zhou, Han, Tang and Ming precedents. The transcription is of the right text but misreads characters in names and allusions, and one sampled page collapses into fragments. The English gives the general sense of the title lists, but its names and its longer prose passages need checking against the image.

title: Tʻonggam chu, Sŏhan chi odae
shelf_note: A Korean manuscript glossary of difficult terms in the Zizhi tongjian (Tonggam), arranged by dynasty from Western Han to the Five Dynasties, with headwords in large script and small double-line glosses. It is a Korean study aid and fits the shelf.
structure_note: 126 pages, 118 translated. The language is labelled 'Korean' but the text is Classical Chinese (I7). Only 13 pages carry printed numbers, so the 3 backsteps and 9 repeats are probably misread numerals or the dynasty labels in the margins (西漢, 唐), not a broken order. The pages are glossaries, not running prose, so a word-by-word English list is the right form; it is not a fault.

book_verdict: The OCR of this Tonggam glossary is usable on the clean pages (98, 79) but weak on the overwritten leaf (23). The English invents allusions and people ('Su Che', 'Di Ku', a Hu mother for Liu Fei, 'Zheng Yu').
reader_summary: A Korean manuscript glossary of hard words in the Zizhi tongjian, from Western Han to the Five Dynasties, with headwords and small glosses. The transcription is of the right text and fair on clean pages, but it flattens the headword/gloss layout and misreads one character in a dozen. The English is a list of glosses that is right in outline, but its proper names and allusions are often invented and must be checked against the image.

title: Sinpʻyŏn Sanhak kyemong
shelf_note: A Korean copy of Zhu Shijie's Suanxue qimeng (1299), the arithmetic primer used for Joseon government mathematics exams. It fits a Korean shelf.
structure_note: 168 pages, 167 with OCR, 154 translated. The language is labelled 'Korean' but the text is Classical Chinese (I7). Pages 38 and 124 are self-tagged 'printed', but the sampled leaves are a handwritten copy (O16). Of the 17 pages with printed numbers, 4 step backwards; this is probably misread folio numerals in the gutter, since the sampled pages run in order (81→83 continue directly).

book_verdict: A clean, legible copy of a central mathematical text, but the OCR gets numbers wrong: a wrong answer on p.38, scrambled tables on p.81, a dropped fraction and a misread rod array on p.124. For a mathematics book, those are the errors that matter. The English sometimes silently corrects the OCR, so the two panes disagree.
reader_summary: This is Zhu Shijie's Suanxue qimeng, the Yuan arithmetic primer the Joseon exam system used, in a Korean copy. The transcription is of the right text, and the prose of the problems and methods is mostly right. The numbers, answers and counting-rod arrays are often wrong, so no answer or worked figure should be trusted without checking the image.
